gardian.c: GARDIAN, or Guardian, signifies generally him that hath the Custody or Charge of any Person or thing ; but most commonly him that hath the h (.location or Protection of such People, as are not of sufficient Discretion to guide themselves and their Affairs, being indeed as largely extended as Tutor and Curator among the Civilians ; for whereas Tutor is he that hath the Government of a Youth, until he come to fourteen Years of Age; and Curator he that hath the imposition and ordering his Estatc afterwards, until he attain to the Age of five and twenty Years; or that hath the Charge of a Erantick Person during his Lunacy,both these with us are called Guardians. A Tutor is either TeJUmcntarius, or a Pratore datus ex Lege Atilia ; or lastly, Lcgitimus : so we have three forts of Guardians in England, one ordained by the Father in his last Will, another appointed by the Judge, the third cast upon the Miner by the Law and Custom of the Land. As to the first of these, a Man having Goods or Chattels, may appoint a Guardian to the Body or Person of his Child, by his Last Will and Testament, until he come to the Age of fourteen Years, and so the disposing and ordering of his Estate, so long as he thinks meet, which is commonly to one and twenty Years of Age. The same he may do of Lands not hoi den in Capite, or by Knights-Service ; but the ancient Law in this cafe is very much altered, and in all cafes, gives the Father power to appoint a Guardian lor his Child ; but if the Father order no Guardian to his Child, the Ordinary may appoint one to manage his Goods and Chattels till the Age of fourteen Years ; at which time he may choose him another Guardian, as by the Civil Law he may his Curator ; for this Rule holds, that is, Invito Curator non datur. And for his Lands the next a-kin on that side, by which the Land cometh not, shall be Guardian who was formerly called Guardian in Soccage.

There are Ten Eminent Circles upon the Globe, or of the Sphere; Six of which are called Greater. and the Four other Lester Circles. A Great Circle of the Sphere is that whose Plane passeth through the Centre of the Sphere, and divides it into two equal Parts or Hemispheres. A Lester Circle, is that which is parallel to a Greater ; as the Tropicks and the Polar Circles, are to the Equator ; and as the Circles of Altitude are to the Horizon. Or Lester Circles are such as do not divide the Globe into two equal parts. The Greater Circles are, I. The Horizon, which is a broad Wooden Circle encompassing the Globe round about, having two Notches, the one in the North, the other in the South part of it, for the Brazen Meridian, to stand in. There are usually accounted two Horizons . First, The Visible or Sensible, which you may conceive to be made by some great Plain, or the Surface of the Sea; and which divides the Heavens into two Hemispheres, the one above, the other (apparently) below the Level of the Earth. This Circle determines the Rising and Setting of the Sun, Moon, or Stars, in any particular Latitude ; for when any one of them comes just to the Eastern edge of the Horizon, then we say it Rifeth ; and when it doth so at the Western edge, we say it Setteth.
